title: Learning Retrieval Models with Sparse Autoencoders
one_liner: Build sparse retrieval features from learned internal units instead of forcing every query and document through a fixed vocabulary list.
lead: Learned sparse retrieval usually represents a query or document by scoring vocabulary items. That is convenient, but it ties retrieval to the words in the vocabulary and limits transfer across languages and domains. This paper uses sparse autoencoders to discover reusable internal features, then uses those sparse feature outputs as retrieval signals. The result is a sparse retriever that stays efficient while transferring better beyond the training data because the learned features can match shared concepts even when surface wording changes.

problem.h2: Why vocabulary-based sparse retrieval tops out
paras: Sparse retrieval is attractive because it is efficient at search time and easy to index. Most learned sparse systems, however, score vocabulary items directly. That means the retrieval space is tied to specific words. When the domain changes or the language changes, useful meaning may not line up cleanly with that fixed word list.

A retrieval feature should capture a concept that can appear in many surface forms. Vocabulary scoring often fragments that concept across many terms, which weakens generalization. The paper's claim is that sparse autoencoders provide a better set of sparse features because they are learned from the model's internal hidden-state patterns rather than from a hand-fixed word inventory.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use sparse autoencoders to discover sparse internal features, then index queries and documents with those features so retrieval stays sparse while transferring across languages and domains.

panels.title: 1. Standard sparse retrieval
panels.viz_args: Query and document -> score vocabulary entries -> compare sparse word lists
panels.caption: The retrieval space is fixed by the vocabulary.

panels.title: 2. A cross-domain or cross-language query appears
panels.caption: Word-level sparsity can miss the match because surface forms differ.

panels.title: 3. Learn sparse internal features
panels.viz_args: Sparse autoencoder turns dense hidden state into a small active feature set
panels.caption: The active features can express recurring concepts beyond a fixed word list.

panels.title: 4. Index with those features
panels.caption: Search now happens in a sparse learned feature space.

panels.title: 5. Transfer improves
panels.caption: Matching improves across languages and domains because the sparse features capture reusable meaning.

steps.b: Step 1: Read hidden states from a language model
steps.text: Take the model's internal activations for queries and documents, because those activations already summarize meaning beyond raw surface words.
Learn a sparse code that reconstructs those activations, so that each item is represented by a small set of active learned features.

steps.b: Step 3: Use the sparse code as the retrieval index
steps.text: Store documents by their active learned features, because a shared feature can connect related items even when they use different wording.

steps.b: Step 4: Encode queries the same way
steps.text: Map each query into the same sparse feature space, so that search compares aligned sparse representations for both sides.

steps.b: Step 5: Rank by sparse feature overlap
steps.text: Return documents with the strongest feature agreement, because those documents activate many of the same learned concepts as the query.

paras: The paper changes the indexing units used by sparse retrieval. Instead of scoring vocabulary entries, it indexes queries and documents with sparse learned features from a sparse autoencoder.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: concept-level match under sparse coding
hidden.name: Sparse feature agreement
paras: A good sparse retriever should match documents that express the same idea even when their wording differs. That hidden quantity is feature agreement at the concept level. If two items activate overlapping sparse learned features, they may belong together even when they share few exact words.

This is especially important for multilingual and out-of-domain retrieval. The same underlying concept can appear under different surface forms. Learned sparse features help because they can fire for recurring internal patterns that cut across wording.

heat.caption: The darker failures happen when word overlap is weak. The learned sparse features try to recover those matches.

reads.html: Feature agreement asks whether the query and the document turn on the same small set of learned concepts.
Sparse autoencoders decompose the model's dense hidden state into sparse learned features, which are then used as indexing units for retrieval.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: sparse learned features generalize better than fixed word slots
paras: The method works because it keeps the efficiency benefits of sparse retrieval while replacing a brittle vocabulary target with learned features. Vocabulary-based methods can only score the words they know. A learned sparse feature can respond to a recurring concept that appears in several languages or domains, so matching survives wording changes.

Sparse autoencoders also preserve search efficiency because each query and document activates only a small subset of features. That keeps the index sparse. The retrieval gain comes from the quality of those active features: they summarize internal language-model structure that already captures semantic regularities, so the sparse overlap is more informative than raw word overlap.

stages.s: Read dense hidden state from the language model
Compress into a sparse learned code
Index and compare active learned features

math.words: Encode the query and each document as sparse feature-value maps, then score a document by summing the products on the active features they share. More shared active features with larger values produce a higher score.
symbols: retrieval score for one query-document pair
the query value on learned feature f
the document value on learned feature f
sum only over features that are active in the sparse codes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a query about battery safety activates three learned features: charging risk, overheating, and product recall.
A relevant document activates charging risk and product recall strongly, so its score is high.
A nonrelevant document activates battery chemistry only weakly and misses the recall feature, so its score stays low.
The match succeeds even if the wording differs, because the overlap is computed on sparse learned features rather than on exact word identity.

math.note: The score can transfer across languages and domains because the sparse feature space is not limited to one vocabulary list.

charts.title: Vocabulary-based learned sparse retrieval
charts.note: Word-linked sparse retrieval works best when test data stays close to the training data, because its sparse scores are tied to the exact vocabulary patterns it learned.

charts.title: Sparse autoencoder retrieval
charts.note: The learned sparse features improve transfer because they encode reusable concept-level structure instead of tying every score to one vocabulary slot.

items.b: The sparse code may become too diffuse.
items.html: If too many features activate at once, indexing loses efficiency because the representation is no longer truly sparse.

items.b: Learned features may be hard to interpret.
items.html: Interpretability is not guaranteed, so some active features may improve retrieval without yielding a simple human label, because the feature may capture a useful mixed concept rather than one tidy category.

items.b: The source language model limits what features can be learned.
items.html: If the underlying hidden states do not separate important distinctions, the sparse autoencoder cannot recover them, because it only reorganizes the information that is already present.

items.b: Done right: sparse retrieval stays fast and transfers better.
items.html: The method succeeds because each item still activates only a small number of learned features, while those features carry more reusable meaning than fixed vocabulary scores.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small retrieval benchmark with parallel query-document pairs from two languages and one held-out domain. Compare a vocabulary-based sparse retriever against a sparse-autoencoder-based retriever built from the same language model's hidden states. Keep the index sparse in both cases. Then measure top-k retrieval across the easy in-domain split and the harder cross-language and held-out-domain splits. The demo should show that the sparse-autoencoder version keeps similar efficiency while improving transfer, because its sparse features capture shared concepts that survive wording changes.
demo.metric_eq: recall_at_k = (# queries with a relevant document in top k) / (# queries)
demo.closing: The demo must show stronger transfer under the same sparse-search budget, because the learned sparse features should preserve concept matches that vocabulary-only scoring misses.
